explanations.answer: The LORD had appeared to David there
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says Solomon built on Mount Moriah, "…where the LORD had appeared to his father David." (2 Chronicles 3:1) So this spot was already special before one stone got stacked. I like a builder who starts with the place God already showed up.

explanations.answer: David had been anointed king there
explanations.explanation: Close, because it's a big David moment, but it isn't the one this verse names. David's anointing is a different story (1 Samuel 16:13). What 2 Chronicles 3:1 says about Mount Moriah is that "…the LORD had appeared to his father David." there. Mixing up David's big moments is easy, friend. The man had a lot of them.

That's a great story, but the text puts it somewhere else. It starts with Saul and the men of Israel camped in the Valley of Elah, facing the Philistines and their champion Goliath (1 Samuel 17:2, 4). This verse says Mount Moriah is where "…the LORD had appeared to his father David." (2 Chronicles 3:1) Same David, different place, friend.

Yes, David. The text says this was "…the place that David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite." (2 Chronicles 3:1) So Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, is building on ground his father got ready. I know a little about being prepared for a job I didn't see coming, friend.

Nathan was a prophet who spoke to David (2 Samuel 7:2), so I see why his name came to mind. But this verse gives the preparing to someone else. It says the place was "…the place that David had prepared…" (2 Chronicles 3:1) Nathan gets a pass on this one, friend.

Samuel was the prophet who anointed David (1 Samuel 16:13), so he's a fair guess. But the text hands this job to David himself. It says the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite was "…the place that David had prepared…" (2 Chronicles 3:1) Samuel's a fair name to reach for, baker, but the job belongs to David.

Right, wing to wing, friend. One wing of the first cherub is five cubits long and touches the wall of the temple, and its other wing is five cubits long and touches the wing of the other cherub. (2 Chronicles 3:11) The second cherub's wings measure the same and touch the wall and the first cherub's wing. (2 Chronicles 3:12) Together the total wingspan is twenty cubits. (2 Chronicles 3:13)

Not heads, baker. The text says the other wing "…touched the wing of the other cherub." (2 Chronicles 3:11) Each cherub has one wing reaching to the wall and one wing reaching to the other cherub. The second cherub's wings do the same. (2 Chronicles 3:12)

Feet are in the passage, but they're doing a different job. The cherubim "…stood on their feet, facing the main room." (2 Chronicles 3:13) The wing that reaches toward the other cherub touches the other cherub's wing. Standing on feet is the only thing the feet get to do here, friend.

True. Each cherub has two wings of five cubits, so the total wingspan is twenty cubits (2 Chronicles 3:11-13). The Most Holy Place is twenty cubits wide (2 Chronicles 3:8). One wing touches one wall, the other cherub's wing touches the opposite wall, and the room is covered, wall to wall. That's some tidy measuring, baker.

The text says otherwise. Their "total wingspan" was twenty cubits, and the Most Holy Place was twenty cubits wide. (2 Chronicles 3:8, 13) One wing of each cherub touches a wall, and the inner wings meet in the middle. So the answer is True, and they do reach wall to wall.

Cherubim it is. Solomon "…made the veil of blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, with cherubim woven into it." (2 Chronicles 3:14) So you've got cherubim on the walls, cherubim in the Most Holy Place and cherubim in the thread. The man had a theme, friend.

Lions would've been a bold choice, but the text doesn't have them on the veil. It says the veil was made of blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, "…with cherubim woven into it." (2 Chronicles 3:14) The walls and the Most Holy Place already had cherubim. The veil follows along.

No eagles on this veil, baker. The text says it was made "…with cherubim woven into it." (2 Chronicles 3:14) It's the same kind of figure Solomon carved on the walls (2 Chronicles 3:7). Eagles can stay up in the sky.

True. The text says Solomon set up the pillars in front of the temple, "The pillar on the south he named Jachin, and the pillar on the north he named Boaz." (2 Chronicles 3:17) These aren't just big columns. They've got names, baker. I was carved with a name too, so I appreciate it.

The text says Solomon did give them names. Verse 17 says he set them up, one on the south and one on the north, and that he named each one. (2 Chronicles 3:17) So the answer is True. Those pillars are not nameless, friend.

Jachin and Boaz. Solomon named the south pillar Jachin and the north pillar Boaz. (2 Chronicles 3:17) Two names, two pillars, one on each side. Say them out loud a couple of times, baker, they're fun.
Half right, and the half is a good one. Jachin is the south pillar. The north pillar is Boaz, not Obed. (2 Chronicles 3:17) I think it's the Bible names that sound alike that get us, friend.

Those names aren't on these pillars, baker. Solomon named the south pillar Jachin and the north pillar Boaz. (2 Chronicles 3:17) Two pillars, two names, one on each side. Next time you pass the front of the temple, you'll know who to wave at.

Oxen, twelve of them. "The Sea stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east." (2 Chronicles 4:4) Their hindquarters pointed to the center, and the Sea rested on them. That's a lot of oxen holding up one very big bowl, baker.

Lions would make for a dramatic entrance, but that isn't what the text says. The Sea stood on twelve oxen, three facing each direction. (2 Chronicles 4:4) There were also ox figures cast in two rows below the rim (2 Chronicles 4:3). It's an ox kind of Sea, friend.

Eagles would be a sight, baker, but the text puts something else under the Sea. It says the Sea rested on twelve oxen, with all their hindquarters toward the center. (2 Chronicles 4:4) Three faced north, three west, three south and three east. It's an ox kind of Sea.

The priests. Verse 6 says the parts of the burnt offering were rinsed in the ten basins, "…but the priests used the Sea for washing." (2 Chronicles 4:6) So there were two sets of washing, each for its own use. The Sea was the priests' tub, baker.

The text doesn't say the king's household used the Sea. Verse 6 says the ten basins were for the burnt offering parts, "…but the priests used the Sea for washing." (2 Chronicles 4:6) So the answer is the priests. Not even the king gets a line here, friend.

The singers aren't mentioned in this verse, baker. The text says, "…but the priests used the Sea for washing." (2 Chronicles 4:6) The basins were for rinsing the burnt offering parts. The Sea belonged to the priests.

The lampstands weren't all stacked on one side. Solomon made ten gold lampstands and placed them in the temple, "…five on the south side and five on the north." (2 Chronicles 4:7) So the statement is False. Five and five, nice and balanced, friend.

False, and good catch. Solomon made ten gold lampstands, but he set "…five on the south side and five on the north." (2 Chronicles 4:7) They were split down the middle, not all on the north. That's an even split, baker.

Bowls, a hundred of them, all gold. The text says, "He also made a hundred gold bowls." (2 Chronicles 4:8) That comes right after the ten tables he placed in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north. Bowls it is, baker.

Cups sound close, but the text says bowls. Solomon made ten tables and set them in the temple, five on each side. Then "He also made a hundred gold bowls." (2 Chronicles 4:8) A hundred is a big number, friend.
No jars on this list, baker. The text says Solomon made ten tables and "…a hundred gold bowls." (2 Chronicles 4:8) They were gold, and there were a hundred of them. Keep the jars for another passage.

explanations.answer: No one could figure out the weight
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker, and the text says so plainly. Solomon made all these articles in such great abundance "…that the weight of the bronze could not be determined." (2 Chronicles 4:18) The pile was so big that no one could settle on a weight for it. I can't even get my cookie dough to the right pound.

Whoa, hold on, friend. The courtyard? The text never says the bronze filled it. It says the articles were made in such great abundance "…that the weight of the bronze could not be determined." (2 Chronicles 4:18) So the real result is that nobody could pin down the weight. If I'd cast that much bronze, my bakery would've needed a bigger planet, baker.

explanations.answer: It used up every mine in Israel
explanations.explanation: Every mine in Israel? Whoa, friend, the text doesn't go there. It says the bronze was made in such great abundance "…that the weight of the bronze could not be determined." (2 Chronicles 4:18) The result is that no one could figure out the weight. That's plenty big without adding mines, baker.

The Bread of the Presence. Solomon made "the tables on which was placed the Bread of the Presence…" (2 Chronicles 4:19) Those tables had a very specific job. A table with a purpose, baker, I respect that.

Incense isn't what the text puts on these tables, baker. Verse 19 says the tables were where "…the Bread of the Presence…" was placed. (2 Chronicles 4:19) Censers do show up later in the list. (2 Chronicles 4:22) The tables get the bread, friend.

The anointing oil isn't mentioned in this passage, baker. The text says the tables were the ones "…on which was placed the Bread of the Presence…" (2 Chronicles 4:19) That's what they held. Bread on the tables, and that's the whole answer.

The lampstands don't burn in the large court. The text says they were "…to burn in front of the inner sanctuary as prescribed…" (2 Chronicles 4:20) The large court is a different place (2 Chronicles 4:9). So the answer is False, friend.

False, and you read it right. The lampstands of pure gold and their lamps were "…to burn in front of the inner sanctuary as prescribed…" (2 Chronicles 4:20) The large court is mentioned earlier, with bronze doors (2 Chronicles 4:9). Different spot, baker.
